passages.t: Jeremiah in the stocks, and Pashhur renamed
passages.happening:
Pashhur the priest, son of Immer and chief officer in the LORD's house, heard Jeremiah's words (verse 1). ‘He had Jeremiah the prophet beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD’ (verse 2).

The next day Pashhur let him out. Jeremiah told him that the LORD does not call him Pashhur but Magor-missabib, terror on every side (verse 3). God will make him a terror to himself and all his friends, and give Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon (verse 4). The wealth and treasures of the city and its kings will be carried to Babylon (verse 5). Pashhur and all his household will go into captivity, and there he will die and be buried with the friends to whom he prophesied lies (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Pashhur was the officer responsible for order in the temple, and Jeremiah had just announced its ruin in its own court (19:14-15). The stocks held a prisoner's feet, and sometimes hands and neck, in a twisted, painful position, set in a public gate where everyone could see and mock.

This is the first time the book names Babylon as the enemy. The foe from the north now has a name.

Pashhur, a priest, had also prophesied. He was one of the voices promising peace. His new name, terror on every side, is the phrase Jeremiah had used of the coming invasion. The man who silenced the warning will live inside it.
passages.later: A psalm of the righteous sufferer says, ‘Among all my enemies I am a disgrace’ (Psalm 31:11). Jeremiah would be beaten and imprisoned again under Zedekiah (Jeremiah 37:15).
passages.asks: Jeremiah was beaten for speaking the truth in the temple. Ask what it might cost you to say something true in a place that does not want to hear it. And ask whether you, like Pashhur, have ever tried to silence a warning instead of heeding it.

passages.happening:
‘You have deceived me, O LORD, and I was deceived. You have overcome me and prevailed’ (verse 7). Jeremiah is a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks him (verse 7). Whenever he speaks he has to cry out violence and destruction, and the word of the LORD has brought him only reproach (verse 8).

If he says he will not speak in God's name any more, ‘His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones, and I become weary of holding it in, and I cannot prevail’ (verse 9).

He hears many whispering, terror on every side, and even his close friends wait for him to slip (verse 10). ‘But the LORD is with me like a fearsome warrior’ (verse 11). His persecutors will stumble. He commits his cause to the God who sees the heart (verse 12). “Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD! For He rescues the life of the needy from the hands of evildoers” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
This is the last and darkest of Jeremiah's confessions. The word translated deceived can also mean enticed or persuaded, as one might persuade a young person. Jeremiah feels that God drew him into a calling he could not have imagined and then overpowered him.

Yet he cannot stop. When he tries to keep quiet, God's word burns in him like a fire shut up in his bones. He is trapped between a message that brings mockery and a fire that will not let him be silent.

The whisper of his friends, terror on every side, turns his own phrase against him. Even those close to him wait for him to fall.

Then, suddenly, praise. Verse 13 is a hymn in the middle of the darkness. And the very next verse falls into the deepest despair in the book.
passages.later: The psalmist knew the same fire: ‘my heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned’ (Psalm 39:3). Paul writes, ‘Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel’ (1 Corinthians 9:16).
passages.asks: Jeremiah could not stop speaking even when it cost him everything. Ask what burns in you that you cannot hold in. And ask whether you can praise God in the middle of a dark season, as Jeremiah did in verse 13.

passages.t: Cursed be the day he was born
passages.happening:
Then the darkness. Jeremiah curses the day he was born, and wishes it had never been counted good (verse 14). He curses the man who brought his father the news of a son's birth and made him glad (verse 15), and wishes that man the fate of the overthrown cities (verse 16), because he did not end Jeremiah's life before he was born (verse 17).

‘Why did I come out of the womb to see only trouble and sorrow, and to end my days in shame?’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The chapter does not soften these words, and these notes do not either. Jeremiah does not ask to die, and he does not harm himself. He cries out that he wishes he had never been born, because his life has been filled with trouble and sorrow and, he fears, will end in shame.

The same cry is found elsewhere in the Bible. Job curses the day of his birth. Moses asks God to take his life, and Elijah sits under a broom tree and prays that he might die. In the stories of Moses and Elijah, God answers with help, food and rest, not condemnation.

The passage ends with a question, and the chapter does not answer it. But Jeremiah's story did not end here. He lived on through siege and exile, and his book goes on to hold some of the greatest words of hope in Scripture.
passages.later: Job spoke the same way: ‘May the day of my birth perish’ (Job 3:3). When Elijah prayed to die, an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat” (1 Kings 19:5).
passages.hard:
How can a prophet of God curse the day he was born, and what does this passage offer someone who feels the same?

Verses 14 to 18 are among the darkest words in the Bible, and they stand in Scripture unexplained and uncorrected. Job says much the same, and so in different ways do Moses (Numbers 11:15) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:4). In their stories God answers with help, food and rest rather than condemnation. The Bible does not treat such words as a failure of faith or diagnose the person who speaks them. It treats them as prayer: words spoken to God by someone who is still, even here, talking to him.

Jeremiah's story did not end in this chapter. He lived on, and his book goes on to contain some of Scripture's greatest words of hope (29:11; 31:31-34).

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jeremiah brought his darkest words to God rather than hiding them. Ask whether there are words you have not dared to say to God. And ask who you could tell, today, if the darkness in you feels like his.
